title: Maintaining Multiple API Versions
learning_outcomes: Explain how maintaining multiple api versions affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from shared business logic across versions to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on maintaining multiple api versions in api versioning and lifecycle management. You will connect shared business logic across versions to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Maintaining Multiple API Versions matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying shared business logic across versions deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 186 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 186: Shared business logic across versions → Version-specific request and response mapping → Avoiding duplicated implementations → Monitoring usage of older versions.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “Maintaining Multiple API Versions” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Maintaining Multiple API Versions
content_blocks.code:
/v1/orders/ord_123
/v2/orders/ord_123

# Example migration note:
# v1 deprecated on 2027-06-01; clients should move to v2.
# Publish actual dates only after usage and support policies are reviewed.
content_blocks.expected_output: A version strategy communicates the contract boundary; deprecation needs a timeline, consumer evidence, and migration documentation.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Shared business logic across versions”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Version-specific request and response mapping” and “Monitoring usage of older versions”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Compatibility is a consumer property; deprecations need evidence, communication, and a migration path. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating maintaining multiple api versions. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating maintaining multiple api versions as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
